subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The parietal lobe is mainly involved in processing what?
options: Touch and sensory information about the body
questions.explain: The parietal lobe processes touch, temperature and sensory information about the body.

questions.q: The cerebellum at the back of the brain is mainly involved in what?
questions.explain: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and posture.

questions.q: A CT (CAT) scan mainly produces what kind of image of the brain?
options: A picture of blood oxygen only
A detailed structural image using X-rays
A real-time map of brain activity
questions.explain: A CT scan uses X-rays to build a detailed structural image of the brain's anatomy.

questions.q: Which type of neuron carries messages from the CNS to muscles to produce movement?
questions.explain: Motor neurons carry signals from the central nervous system to muscles and glands to cause action.

questions.q: Which lobe contains the primary auditory area for processing sound?
questions.explain: The temporal lobe contains the auditory cortex, which processes sound and is involved in hearing.

questions.q: The autonomic nervous system is divided into which two branches?
questions.explain: The autonomic nervous system has sympathetic (arousing) and parasympathetic (calming) branches.

questions.q: Which part of a neuron RECEIVES signals from other neurons?
questions.explain: Dendrites are the branch-like structures that receive incoming signals from other neurons.

questions.q: Chemicals released to carry a signal across the synapse are called what?
questions.explain: Neurotransmitters are the chemical messengers that diffuse across the synapse between neurons.

questions.q: 'Localisation of function' is the idea that what?
options: Specific areas of the brain have specific functions
The whole brain does every task equally
Only the left side of the brain works
questions.explain: Localisation of function is the theory that particular areas of the brain are responsible for particular functions.

questions.q: What is the tiny gap between two neurons across which messages pass called?
questions.explain: The synapse is the small gap between neurons where neurotransmitters carry the signal across.

questions.q: Within a single neuron, how is the signal transmitted?
questions.explain: Inside a neuron the signal travels as an electrical impulse along the axon.

questions.q: The peripheral nervous system includes which division that controls voluntary muscle movement?
questions.explain: The somatic nervous system controls voluntary movements of skeletal muscles.

questions.q: What is the role of the myelin sheath on a neuron?
options: To speed up the electrical impulse along the axon
questions.explain: The myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds up the transmission of the electrical impulse.

questions.q: The case of Phineas Gage, who survived a rod through his frontal lobe, suggests the frontal lobe is linked to what?
questions.explain: Gage's personality change after frontal-lobe damage supports the lobe's role in personality and behaviour.

questions.q: During fight-or-flight, what typically happens to the heart rate?
questions.explain: The sympathetic response increases heart rate to pump more blood and oxygen to the muscles.

questions.q: Which lobe of the brain is mainly responsible for processing vision?
questions.explain: The occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, is mainly responsible for processing visual information.

questions.q: During fight-or-flight, which hormone is released to prepare the body for action?
questions.explain: Adrenaline is released, raising heart rate and energy to prepare the body for fight or flight.

questions.q: Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's ability to do what?
options: Change and reorganise itself through experience
questions.explain: Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change and form new connections in response to experience.

questions.q: Which brain-scanning technique measures blood flow to show active brain areas?
questions.explain: fMRI detects changes in blood flow and oxygenation to show which brain areas are active.

questions.q: Which brain structure plays a key role in forming new long-term memories?
questions.explain: The hippocampus is crucial for forming and consolidating new long-term memories.

questions.q: After a threat has passed, which branch returns the body to a resting state?
questions.explain: The parasympathetic branch calms the body, slowing heart rate and restoring it to rest.

questions.q: Which lobe is most associated with higher functions like reasoning, planning and personality?
questions.explain: The frontal lobe handles higher cognitive functions such as reasoning, planning and personality.
